options.text: The electorate moved from a sweeping mandate for one candidate to an almost even split between the parties.

options.misconception: Third-party support fell, but it never decided these elections; Perot's 18.9 percent in 1992 won no electors.
options.text: The electorate moved from supporting third-party candidates in large numbers to supporting only the two major parties.

options.misconception: The parties traded wins: Republicans won 1980 through 1988, Democrats won 1992 and 1996, and a Republican won 2000.
options.text: The electorate moved from favoring Democratic candidates to favoring Republican candidates in every single election.

options.misconception: The table says nothing about what issues moved voters; vote shares alone cannot show which issue mattered most.
options.text: The electorate moved from voting mainly on foreign policy issues to voting mainly on economic issues.

rationales.A:
In 1984 Reagan won 525 electoral votes and nearly 59 percent of the vote; in 2000 the winner took 271 electors while losing the popular vote. Background: the 2000 result was so close that the Supreme Court's decision in Bush v. Gore settled the presidency.
A 49-state landslide and a 537-vote Florida margin are two different countries, politically speaking — one sure of itself, one split down the middle.
rationales.B: Third-party support fell, but it never decided these elections. Background: Perot's 18.9 percent in 1992 won no electors, and by 2000 the third-party share was small.
rationales.C: The parties traded wins: Republicans won 1980 through 1988, Democrats won 1992 and 1996, and a Republican won 2000. Background: the table shows alternation, not a steady move toward either party.
rationales.D: The table says nothing about what issues moved voters. Background: issues mattered in every election here, but vote shares alone cannot show which issue mattered most.
rationales.general:
1. Put the two rows side by side. 1984: 525 electors, 58.8 percent. 2000: 271 electors, 47.9 percent — and the loser won more votes.
2. Ask what changed between them. Not the parties — both won elections in between.
3. Ask what the closeness means. Background: the 2000 election came down to a few hundred votes in Florida and a Supreme Court decision.
4. Name the shift. From landslide to dead heat, the country went from speaking with one voice to speaking with two.
Remember: 1984 was a verdict; 2000 was a tie that the courts had to break.

stem: Comparing the elections of 1984 and 2000 in the table, which of the following best describes the change in American politics?

stimulus.source_note: Data from the American Presidency Project, via the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History.
stimulus.text:
Presidential election results, 1980–2000:

| Year | Winner | Winner's popular vote | Runner-up's popular vote | Winner's electoral votes |
| 1980 | Ronald Reagan (R) | 50.7% | Carter 41.0% | 489 |
| 1984 | Ronald Reagan (R) | 58.8% | Mondale 40.6% | 525 |
| 1988 | George H. W. Bush (R) | 53.4% | Dukakis 45.6% | 426 |
| 1992 | Bill Clinton (D) | 43.0% | Bush 37.4% | 370 |
| 1996 | Bill Clinton (D) | 49.2% | Dole 40.7% | 379 |
| 2000 | George W. Bush (R) | 47.9% | Gore 48.4% | 271 |

Ross Perot, running as an independent, won 18.9% of the popular vote in 1992 and 8.4% in 1996, winning no electoral votes in either year.
